messages.subject: Occupancy models with very low or high occupancy associated with certain covariates - fix estimates?
messages.subject_clean: Occupancy models with very low or high occupancy associated with certain covariates - fix estimates?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am running occupancy models on birds using habitat type as a nominal covariate. There are 8 habitat types in my dataset, with 7-11 replicates of each habitat type. There were six surveys for each site. For many species, there are either no detections, or naive occupancy = 1, either of which resulting in huge standard errors on my estimates.

Is there a way to set the estimate/psi at something very close to 0 or very close to 1 (depending on whether there are 0 detections or naive occ = 1) so that I can run the models, get realistic estimates, and reasonable answers for model selection? I have been struggling with using the "offset" function, thus far with no success.

I appreciate any advice! Thank you,

Isabel

messages.subject: Is stacking data possible for within year-different month observations?
messages.subject_clean: Is stacking data possible for within year-different month observations?
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I have a question regarding a bird species data set and the possibility of it being analyzed to obtain N (abundance) for an area. I know the routes this could be done in unmarked: "gdistsamp", "occuRN", "pcount"; each follow specific models from their associated articles.  To summarize the information:

- Method: fixed-radius point count
- Sites 178
- Visits 3 (but these visits were spread out in 1 year time: first visit january, second visit march-april, third visit jun-jul)

This is a resident bird species which remains within the geographic area and although it is not certain if it disperses due to little information available (as some species might do in search of food), we didnt see a real difference in contacts per bout (they were pretty equal). I believe the species remains within the surveyed sites. However, the assumption that the population is closed cannot be met because sometime during the year their would be a breeding season, so there would be births and deaths in a year-cycle.

>From what I have encountered in the group, people have had a similar situation where they survey in multiple years. The suggestion in these cases has included "stacking the data"

Would this be something I could do? I think that the advantage that other people have is that they have their three or more visits per year so if they stack the data they have replications per site, in my case stacking the data would result in 1 count bouts, correct?

Thanks in advance for any comment, suggestion or direction to authors/materials. And thanks to all users and authors in this group, it is definitely different from other groups, I have learned a lot in the past few weeks from the questions, answers, suggestions and articles recommended.

Best

Fabiola R

Fabiola,

Other folks can chime in here, but I think for at least pcount, IF you are willing to assume that births and deaths occur at equal rates across sites, you can still assume closure (Seber 1973).  That's a pretty big assumption depending on your sites and research questions, but the value of repeated surveys at each site will really strengthen your results if you think you can honestly make the assumption above.  If your sites differ by some covariate like habitat type, I THINK you could extend the assumption to equal birth and death rates within a habitat type provided your models account for habitat type.  But I'd be curious if others would agree with that statement.

-Alex W.

hi Fabiola,
 I assume you used a normal point count protocol and NOT distance sampling or time-removal or similar.
 In that case , due to the long time span of the counts, the population is certainly not closed in this time.
 You could fit the Dail-Madsen model (pcountOpen in unmarked) but note this is a pretty advanced model and very sensitive to sparse data and the specific model assumptions that underlie it. You should do a lot of reading on the model and proceed cautiously.

regards,
andy

Hello all,

Noted.

Distance (meters) to individual was taken as we wanted to assess when we'd stop detecting the individuals, as well as to know what would be our circular plot limit to take some vegetation structure and composition metrics to characterize the habitat. We also recorded the first interval of detection to assess if our 10 minute count is OK or if less would suffice for future surveys. But, unfortunately we did not keep "ticking" interval boxes if an individual remained throughout the counts, records are based on first-contact only. So I believe that this is what you mean when you mention time-removal, correct?

Thank you for your responses. All part of the learning experience for sure.

Fabiola R.

messages.body_plain:
Dear unmarked group,

I fit a single season occupancy model using occu(). The model has a quadratic effect of elevation. Both elevation and elevation2 variables were standardized.

fm3=occu(~1~elevation+elevation2, sangelae)

Call:

occu(formula = ~1 ~ elevation + elevation2, data = sangelae)

Occupancy:

            Estimate    SE     z P(>|z|)

(Intercept)     0.72 0.473  1.52 0.12799

elevation       2.17 0.979  2.22 0.02647

elevation2     -3.31 1.082 -3.06 0.00225

Detection:

 Estimate    SE    z  P(>|z|)

      1.3 0.191 6.84 8.06e-12

AIC: 227.7983

Now I want to get predictions for this model.

sangelae.site

newdata1 <- data.frame(sangelae.site)

newdata1

Epsi1 <- predict(fm3, type="state", newdata=newdata1)

Epsi1

y = Epsi1$Predicted

y

y.Err=1.96*Epsi1$SE

y.Up= y + y.Err

y.Dn = y - y.Err

with(Epsi1, {

  plot(1:60, Predicted,type="l", lty=1,lwd=2,col="black",xaxt="n", xlim=c(0.5, 60.5), ylim=c(0, 1),xlab="Elevation (m)",

       ylab=expression(paste("Probability of occurrence (", psi, ")")),

       cex.lab=1,mgp=c(2.3,1,0),

       pch=16, cex=1.5)

  axis(1, 1:60)

})

polygon(c(1:60,rev(1:60)),c(y.Up,rev(y.Dn)),col=rgb(64,64,64,25,maxColorValue=255),border=rgb(192,192,192,25,maxColorValue=255))

By mistake I used my own data set as “newdata” and I was able to obtain a nice curve with higher probability of occupancy at middle elevations. Obviously this is not a prediction. I think that, in this case, I`m seeing the data backtrasformed, right?

Then I tried again, with a new data set:

newdata7 <- data.frame(elevation=seq(-1.8920,1.4434,length.out=60),elevation2=seq(3.57,2.083,length.out=60))

newdata7

Epsi7 <- predict(fm3, type="state", newdata=newdata7,appendData=TRUE)

Epsi7

plot(Predicted ~ elevation2, Epsi7, type="l", ylim=c(-0.1, 1.1),

     xlab="Elevation2",

     ylab="Expected occupancy probability")

lines(lower ~elevation2, Epsi7, type="l", col=gray(0.5))

lines(upper ~elevation2, Epsi7, type="l", col=gray(0.5))

But, now my predictions are incredible low and I never get a quadratic curve.

I already tried to hold one covariate as constant without success.

Anyone can help me with this?

Thanks

Best

Marconi Campos

Hi Travis et al,

I thought I share some code as well here as it seems fitting. The attached file includes a function that fits model combinations, but other than dredge it does not fit all possible combinations but rather searches the model space using AIC values. For each iteration of the outer loop it tries to fit a model adding (in this case) site specific covariates on the psi side, lists them, compares AIC values and retains the models within AICcut from the top model for the next iteration. It also tests for model convergence and NAN's. Its a work in progress but I have used and worked on this sporadically over the last couple years, so hopefully its somewhat tested. It would be great if others that find this useful could give it a try and let me know what they think or if there are any bugs apparent.

Below example code of how to use the function.

Cheers,
Richard

source("f.AIC_cut.occu.sig.used.15.08.11.r")

covar <- read.csv("site_covars.csv")
obs.covar <- read.csv("obs_covars.csv")
SiteCovarSet<-as.vector(c("SC1","SC2","SC3","SC4","SC5"))

MyOccuData<- unmarkedFrameOccu(y,siteCovs=covar, obsCov=obs.covar)

um.frame <- MyOccuData
fm.p <- occu(~OC1+OC2+OC3 ~1, data=um.frame)

#use function from sourced file above
f.occ <- f.AICc.occu.sig(fm.p, SiteCovarSet, max.iter=20, AICcut=2, ,um.frame=MyOccuData)

#optional: remove models where p-values for estimates are higher than p.crit
f.occ.sig <- occu.rem.non.sig(f.occ,p.crit=0.15)
f.occ.sig.sub <- occu.subset(f.occ.sig,cutoff=7)

#model averaging: the else part is only needed if f.AICc.occu.sig returned only one model
if (length(f.occ.sig.sub)>1){
  f.occ.avg <- model.avg(f.occ.sig.sub)
  f.occ.avg <- add.coefmat(f.occ.avg)
} else {
  f.occ.avg <- f.occ.sig.sub

}

I am hoping that someone can help out with a general question with using UNMARKED for abundance (pcount) or occupancy (occu) analysis. Let's say we've sampled 50 survey stations in a defined study area by making replicate visits (n= 3) to each station to collect avian point count data. If a given species is found to occur at all of the survey stations, are there any mathematical limitations or problems that one should anticipate? In most situations such sampling would usually produce a data set that would have 3 types of sites: those known to have 1 or more birds, those with no birds, and those with 1 or more birds but where no detections occurred. However, if all sites are found to be occupied by detecting at least one individual at each site during at least one of the visits, then there are no sites in the data set with encounter histories that comprise only zeros {000}, but a number of sites could still have zeros produced during one or more visits {e.g.,102; one bird on first visit, zero birds on second visit and 2 birds on visit three}. I am wondering if such data would cause any problems during abundance estimation?

I did see a similar post by Igor Berkunsky about employing the unmarked fitting function occu when all sites are known to be occupied, but here I am interested in a similar question but regarding abundance estimation with the pcount function.

Many thanks to everyone contributing to this group, I have found lots of useful information here...but was still unable to answer my question I posed above.

Thanks,

Kiel Drake
Waterbird Scientist
Bird Studies Canada

hi Kiel,

 In such cases I would say that it is almost pointless to fit occupancy models for the simple reason that your data set has no variation in occupancy state to model! That said, you might be interested in explicit models of the detection process which would still be valid. Note, however, that the occu() and related functions will probably produce strange looking errors and apparent non-convergence or singular Hessian matrices because the occupancy intercept parameter is at the boundary of the parameter space.  Be warned.

 It is probably more fruitful in the case to fit the N-mixture model using the pcount() function.

regards
andy

 it is possible to have a basic identifiability problem in this class of models if there is too much heterogeneity within or among sites.  I'm guessing this is the situation you have.
Some relevant discussion appears in this paper:
http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/biom.12246/pdf

A good diagnostic of this problem is what you're observing: as you increase K you do not obtain stable MLEs.
regards,
andy

Javan

messages.body_plain:
Dear Javan,

I think you confuse a couple of things. One is goodness of fit, the other is model selection and the third one is prediction, in particular the computation of the uncertainty around predictions. You seem to want to inflate the prediction standard errors or confidence intervals by the additional uncertainty represented by a c.hat, which you obtain in a Gof test. You can’t do that with unmarked’s own predict function. However, Marc Mazerolle’s AICcmodavg package has a number of very useful functions that work specifically for unmarked fitted objects and includes functions for prediction with inflated SEs/CIs. To be honest, I don’t know whether this also applies to occupancy models, but it does for N-mixture models. I attach a blurb from our upcoming AHM book that describes prediction for Nmix models fit with pcount() and assume that something similar works also for occupancy models fit with occu().

Kind regards  --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Dear Javan,

Here is part 2 of my reply (I should have read your email till the end, sorry !). To get 95% prediction intervals that are inflated by some c.hat value, you can predict on the link scale, the code for and result of which may look something like this:

> modavgPred(cand.set = list(fm12), newdata=newData, parm.type = "detect",

+ type = "link", c.hat = 3.04) # Could be used to get 95% CIs

Model-averaged predictions based on entire model set:

    mod.avg.pred uncond.se <http://uncond.se>

1           0.58      0.56

2           0.53      0.52

3           0.49      0.48

4           0.45      0.45

5           0.41      0.43

6           0.37      0.41

Then you can take the mean plus/minus twice that SE and backtransform (apply the inverse logit) and this will give you approximate, c-hat inflated 95% prediction intervals.

Best regards  --- Marc
